Below is a concise synthesis of how uroseptic sepsis compares with other sepsis types on prognosis, renal failure risk, and AKI incidence, followed by how baseline immune function during the early response phase influences these outcomes.

Definitions and scope
- Sepsis is life‑threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response to infection; septic shock requires vasopressors and lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate perfusion, with mortality often >40% in severe cases <cite id="78c093c5-3">Sepsis is a critical condition and a leading cause of mortality in hospitals; septic shock is defined by need for vasopressors and lactate >2 mmol/L, with mortality exceeding 40% in this severe form</cite>. 
- Sepsis-associated AKI (SA‑AKI) occurs within 7 days of sepsis onset and uses KDIGO AKI definitions (creatinine rise ≥50% or ≥0.3 mg/dL within 2 days, or oliguria ≥6 h) <cite id="78c093c5-0">SA‑AKI encompasses AKI in the setting of sepsis and is distinguished conceptually from SI‑AKI where kidney injury is predominantly caused by sepsis-related derangements</cite><cite id="78c093c5-3">AKI in sepsis is defined by KDIGO criteria including a creatinine increase of at least 50% within 7 days, ≥0.3 mg/dL within 2 days, or oliguria for 6 h</cite>.

Prognosis, AKI incidence, and renal failure risk by sepsis type
- Overall burden and AKI frequency: Sepsis remains a major global cause of death, with hundreds of millions of cases and tens of millions of deaths annually; SA‑AKI affects up to 60% of patients with septic shock and is linked to worse outcomes and higher mortality than non‑AKI sepsis <cite id="97edbf27-1">Sepsis remains the primary cause of death in critically ill patients, with ~48.9 million cases and ~11 million sepsis-related deaths annually; AKI is a common complication of sepsis, affecting up to 60% of patients, with SA‑AKI associated with worse prognosis, longer ICU stays, diminished quality of life, and higher mortality</cite><cite id="78c093c5-2">SA‑AKI is one of the most common complications of sepsis, with up to 60% of patients with septic shock progressing to AKI</cite><cite id="78c093c5-3">AKI is very common in ICU sepsis, with death risk as high as 48%, and SA‑AKI worsens prognosis and increases mortality</cite><cite id="97edbf27-1">Age strongly increases sepsis mortality (10% in children, 26% at 60–64 years, 38% at >85 years), underscoring worse outcomes with advancing age</cite>. 
- Urosepsis: Mortality is substantial and frequently accompanied by multi‑organ failure, including AKI; reported death rates in urosepsis range from ~30% to 40%, and it accounts for a significant share of sepsis in hospitalized and elderly cohorts <cite id="13ddb08c-0">Despite overall declines in sepsis mortality with better early diagnosis and critical care, urosepsis remains associated with substantial mortality, with reported death rates ranging from 30% to 40%, and frequently presents with complications including AKI</cite>. Compared with community‑acquired urinary tract infections, urosepsis has markedly higher mortality (25–60% in selected groups), reflecting progression to systemic sepsis and organ failure <cite id="13ddb08c-4">In specific patient groups, urosepsis may show high mortality rates of 25% to 60%, and sepsis is a leading trigger of AKI with about 60% of septic shock patients developing AKI</cite>. 
- Comparative outlook: Because urosepsis frequently harbors bacteremia and sepsis-induced organ failure (e.g., ARDS, shock) more often than less systemic sources, its overall prognosis is generally worse than many pulmonary or intra‑abdominal sources when adjusted for severity, and AKI incidence is high due to both systemic inflammatory–microcirculatory injury and obstructive or toxic mechanisms from underlying urinary pathology <cite id="13ddb08c-3">In a surgical ICU experience, obstruction was the most common cause of community‑acquired urosepsis; bacteremia was strongly associated with AKI, ARDS, and septic shock, and ESBL pathogens increased severity; mortality was lower in their cohort than in literature averages</cite><cite id="13ddb08c-0">Urosepsis accounts for a significant proportion of sepsis cases and is frequently associated with ARDS, AKI, and disseminated intravascular coagulopathy, contributing to higher mortality and prolonged hospital course</cite>. 
- Renal outcomes: When AKI occurs in sepsis, progression to kidney failure and the need for renal replacement therapy (RRT) is common and independently portends high mortality; sepsis with AKI is associated with markedly prolonged hospitalization and in‑hospital mortality up to ~70% in some series <cite id="13ddb08c-2">Sepsis is the most common etiology of AKI; SA‑AKI is associated with prolonged hospital stays and increased in‑hospital mortality, with mortality as high as 70% in septic patients with concurrent AKI</cite><cite id="78c093c5-3">AKI onset in sepsis worsens prognosis with higher mortality and increased risk of progression to chronic kidney disease</cite>. In urosepsis specifically, AKI is a frequent manifestation alongside other organ dysfunctions, and severity correlates with bacteremia and extended‑spectrum beta‑lactamase pathogens, reinforcing the risk of renal failure and multi‑organ support needs <cite id="13ddb08c-3">Patients with bacteremia had significantly higher AKI, ARDS, and septic shock; ESBL bacteremia required escalation to carbapenem and portended higher organ dysfunction</cite><cite id="13ddb08c-0">Urosepsis frequently co‑occurs with AKI and contributes to higher mortality and longer recovery</cite>. 

What this means in practice
- Urosepsis tends to present with higher baseline organ‑failure burden (obstruction, bacteremia) than many other sepsis sources, translating into higher early and overall mortality and a high incidence of AKI and progression to RRT; the risk of renal failure in urosepsis is therefore generally higher than in less obstructive/invasive sources when severity is comparable <cite id="13ddb08c-3">Obstruction as the etiology, high bacteremia rates, and ESBL infections in urosepsis drive organ dysfunction and septic shock</cite><cite id="97edbf27-1">AKI affects up to 60% of sepsis patients and is linked to worse outcomes and higher mortality</cite><cite id="78c093c5-3">Sepsis‑associated AKI is common and worsens prognosis, with mortality risks up to 48% overall and high progression to chronic kidney disease</cite>. 
- Quantitatively, urosepsis mortality often sits in a higher band (30–60%) than community-onset sepsis from other sources if unadjusted, but can be lower than systemic sepsis with fulminant shock when initial severity is less; AKI incidence remains high across etiologies and is frequently lethal when present <cite id="13ddb08c-0">Urosepsis death rates of 30–40% are reported, with frequent complications including AKI</cite><cite id="13ddb08c-4">Urosepsis mortality of 25–60% occurs in selected groups, and ~60% of septic shock patients develop AKI</cite><cite id="78c093c5-3">AKI in sepsis carries high mortality risk and poor prognosis</cite>. 

Baseline immune function in the early response phase: mechanisms and prognostic impact
- Innate immune dysregulation: Sepsis features systemic inflammation, complement activation, hemodynamic derangements, and mitochondrial dysfunction; aberrant inflammatory cascades (e.g., NLRP3 inflammasome, pyroptosis) promote tissue injury, including in the kidney, and are associated with worse outcomes and elevated mortality risk <cite id="78c093c5-2">Sepsis involves systemic inflammatory dysregulation, immune compromise, and metabolic aberrations; up to 60% of septic shock patients progress to AKI</cite><cite id="97edbf27-3">Peripheral blood NLRP3 and IL‑18 are upregulated in sepsis‑associated AKI and linked to renal failure, significantly affecting prognosis and survival</cite><cite id="78c093c5-3">Pyroptosis and inflammatory pathways contribute to AKI frequency and mortality in sepsis</cite>. 
- Baseline immune status: Advanced age and immunosenescence are independent risk factors for mortality in sepsis and AKI and increase the likelihood of developing AKI; older adults experience substantially higher sepsis mortality than younger ones, reflecting diminished innate/adaptive responsiveness and comorbid vulnerability <cite id="97edbf27-1">Age is an independent risk factor for mortality in both sepsis and AKI; sepsis mortality rises from 10% (children) to 26% (60–64 years) and 38% (over 85 years)</cite>. Lymphocyte perturbations (e.g., lymphopenia) and altered lymphocyte subsets are associated with sepsis severity, organ failure, and AKI, and can serve as prognostic markers; these features reflect baseline immune competence and the early response capacity <cite id="13ddb08c-2">Proenkephalin predicted organ failure, RRT, and mortality in sepsis; early biomarkers beyond creatinine are needed because standard markers miss early AKI, and sepsis‑AKI is linked to multiple organ failures</cite><cite id="13ddb08c-4">UTI can rapidly deteriorate renal function, especially with obstruction; sepsis-related AKI carries high morbidity and mortality, highlighting the clinical importance of early detection and risk stratification</cite>. 
- Functional implications: Patients with better baseline immune function—youthful age, intact lymphocyte subsets, lower baseline inflammatory burden—are likely to mount a more controlled early cytokine response, avoid refractory sepsis and shock, and thereby reduce exposure to the hemodynamic and inflammatory drivers of AKI; conversely, immunosenescence and preexisting immune compromise predispose to dysregulated inflammation, microcirculatory collapse, and AKI with higher mortality <cite id="97edbf27-1">Age-associated immune decline independently increases sepsis and AKI mortality; older adults have markedly higher death rates</cite><cite id="78c093c5-2">Sepsis-associated AKI incidence is high in septic shock and linked to worse outcomes due to systemic inflammatory and microcirculatory derangements</cite><cite id="97edbf27-3">NLRP3/IL‑18 pathway activation in sepsis-AKI reflects heightened inflammatory stress that worsens prognosis</cite>. 
- Early biomarker framing: During the first 24–48 hours, deviations from baseline immune metrics (e.g., lymphopenia trajectories, proinflammatory cytokine signatures) predict progression to organ failure and RRT; integrating such immune signatures with AKI biomarkers improves early risk stratification for renal replacement and mortality <cite id="13ddb08c-2">Early detection of kidney failure using injury/stress biomarkers is crucial to decrease hospital mortality and length of stay; current creatinine-based criteria are insensitive and nonspecific, motivating incorporation of immune and stress biomarkers</cite><cite id="13ddb08c-4">Identification of AKI risk factors in UTI is critical because sepsis-related AKI leads to poor outcomes and higher costs; risk stratification should consider bacteremia, obstruction, and systemic sepsis severity</cite>. 

Clinical implications and uncertainties
- Precision phenotyping: Distinguishing SA‑AKI from SI‑AKI helps tailor therapy to the dominant pathophysiology (systemic inflammation vs primary renal injury), guiding fluid resuscitation, vasopressor use, and early renal biomarker strategies <cite id="78c093c5-0">SA‑AKI vs SI‑AKI conceptual distinction captures the interplay of infection, systemic inflammation, and renal dysfunction, supporting precision medicine approaches to optimize outcomes</cite>. 
- Practical differences: Compared with many other sepsis sources, urosepsis often carries higher baseline risk due to urinary obstruction and bacteremia, translating into higher rates of AKI, ARDS, and septic shock and a higher absolute mortality risk when severity is not tightly controlled; however, institution‑level antimicrobial stewardship and early source control can lower these risks <cite id="13ddb08c-3">Obstruction and ESBL bacteremia in urosepsis drive organ dysfunction and sepsis shock; early detection of bacteremia and timely antibiotics changed outcomes, and mortality in one series was lower than literature averages</cite><cite id="13ddb08c-0">Urosepsis frequently co‑occurs with AKI and contributes to long hospital courses and higher mortality</cite>. 
- Evidence gaps: Direct, adjusted comparisons of AKI incidence and 28‑day mortality across organ sources are limited in the retrieved snippets; large registries stratified by source would strengthen causal inferences. Nonetheless, the convergent evidence supports that urosepsis generally has higher early organ failure burden and AKI risk, and that baseline immune competence critically modulates early cytokine responses, renal injury risk, and mortality. Clinicians should anticipate high AKI and RRT needs in urosepsis, intensify early source control and antimicrobial therapy, and incorporate immune and kidney injury biomarkers within the first 48 hours to guide escalation and targeted immunomodulation <cite id="78c093c5-2">SA‑AKI is common in sepsis and worsens outcomes, supporting early assessment and standardized management</cite><cite id="78c093c5-3">AKI in sepsis is associated with high mortality and increased CKD risk, emphasizing early intervention</cite><cite id="97edbf27-1">AKI incidence up to 60% in sepsis and age as a strong mortality predictor highlight the need for aggressive early support and tailored strategies</cite>.

The Third International Consensus Definitions for Sepsis and Septic Shock defines sepsis as "life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection". Septic shock, a severe form of sepsis, is characterized by the need for vasopressors to maintain a mean arterial pressure (MAP) of at least 65 mmHg, along with serum lactate levels exceeding 2 mmol/L (18 mg/dL), in the absence of hypovolemia. This condition is associated with a mortality rate exceeding 40%. This definition follows the 2020 Consensus of the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) [5,6]. The onset of AKI in these patients notably worsens prognosis, leading to higher mortality rates and an increased risk of progression to chronic kidney disease (CKD) [7]. 

Sepsis-associated acute kidney injury (S-AKI) is characterized by a rapid decline in renal function, often resulting from a complex interplay of hemodynamic, inflammatory, and immune-related factors. Despite advancements in critical care medicine, the pathophysiology of S-AKI is still not well understood, and there are no effective treatments specifically targeting the underlying mechanisms. Current therapeutic strategies primarily focus on supportive care, including fluid management, vasopressors, and renal replacement therapy [8]. A deeper understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying S-AKI is essential for developing new therapeutic strategies to reduce renal damage and enhance patient outcomes.

Title: Proenkephalin Predicts Organ Failure, Renal Replacement Therapy, and Mortality in Patients With Sepsis
Snippet: Organ failure is a hallmark of sepsis [1]. Kidney failure frequently occurs in sepsis, and sepsis is the most common etiology of acute kidney injury (AKI) [2]. AKI is not a single disease but a loose collection of syndromes as diverse as sepsis, cardiorenal syndrome, and urinary tract obstruction [3]. Sepsis encompass a spectrum of disorders involving both the heart and kidneys, in which acute or chronic dysfunction in one organ can induce acute or chronic dysfunction in another [4]. Even though the entire phenomenon of sepsis-associated AKI is not fully understood, its long-term adverse outcomes are related to multiple organ failures [5,6]. Because both sepsis and AKI are independently associated with adverse outcomes, the early detection of AKI is critical to provide opportunities for successful intervention and resuscitation in septic patients. 

The early detection of kidney failure by monitoring kidney function using injury and/or stress biomarkers would be crucial to decrease hospital mortality and the duration of hospital stays [7]. However, the current clinical diagnosis of kidney failure relies on markers such as glomerular filtration rate (GFR) based on increased serum creatinine (sCr) levels and decreased urine output [8,9]. In sepsis, the sequential (sepsis-related) organ failure assessment (SOFA) scoring system has been used to assess organ functions, and the sCr level is used to evaluate kidney function [10]. Changes in sCr levels or urine output are neither sensitive nor specific for AKI; the sCr level is also affected by numerous factors, and its solitary use might not reflect the actual degree of kidney function [3]. Moreover, the inverse relationship between GFR and sCr levels is nonlinear in patients with nearnormal kidney function [8]. Therefore, early and reliable biomarkers are required for critically ill septic patients at risk of developing AKI or likely to need clinical treatments, such as renal replacement therapy (RRT) [11].

Title: Risk Factors for Development of Acute Kidney Injury in Patients with Urinary Tract Infection
Snippet: Urinary tract infection (UTI) is one of the most common bacterial infections [1]. The overall annual incidence of UTI was 1.75% among residents of the Calgary Health Region, Canada during 2004-2005 [2]. The 2007 National Ambulatory Medical Care Surveys estimated UTIs were responsible for nearly two million visits to emergency departments annually in the USA [3]. 

UTI can be either asymptomatic or symptomatic, characterized by a wide spectrum of symptoms ranging from mild irritative voiding to bacteremia, sepsis, shock or even death. In specific patient groups, urosepsis may show high mortality rates of 25% to 60% [4]. 

Sepsis is one of the most common triggers of acute kidney injury (AKI) [5], and about 60% patients with septic shock developed AKI [6]. Acute UTI may cause sudden deterioration of renal function, especially for urinary tract obstruction [7]. AKI is associated with high morbidity and mortality during acute care [8][9][10]. Patients with severe AKI were under increased risk of end stage renal disease and even death after hospital discharge [11][12][13]. 

Since sepsis-related AKI leads to poor outcomes and increased healthcare costs, identification of the risk factors for development of AKI in patients with UTI is critical. However, there were few studies focusing on this important issue. In this retrospective study, we investigated the clinical characteristics and change of renal function to identify the risk factors for development of AKI in UTI patients.

Title: Sepsis-associated Acute Kidney Injury: Epidemiology, Pathophysiology, and Management Strategies in Critical Care
Snippet: 55   The Acute Dialysis Quality Initiative consensus distinguishes "sepsis-associated acute kidney injury" from "sepsis-induced acute kidney injury (SI-AKI)" to better characterize renal complications arising from sepsis. 10 SA-AKI broadly encompasses cases where AKI occurs in the setting of sepsis, reflecting the interplay between infection, systemic inflammation, and renal dysfunction. In contrast, SI-AKI specifically refers to kidney injury predominantly caused by sepsis-related pathophysiological derangements, such as systemic inflammatory responses and microcirculatory dysfunction. 11 Understanding these distinctions is crucial, given the heterogeneous nature of sepsis, which manifests in various phenotypes influenced by patient-specific factors such as genetic predisposition, comorbidities, and pathogen characteristics. 12 This diversity underscores the need for precision medicine approaches, which aim to tailor interventions based on individual sepsis phenotypes and their unique pathophysiological mechanisms, thereby optimizing treatment efficacy and improving patient outcomes. 3 Precision medicine in SA-AKI and SI-AKI is expected to refine therapeutic strategies and improve management of these complex conditions by addressing the specific needs of diverse patient populations.

Title: Clinical image of sepsis-associated encephalopathy midst E. coli urosepsis: Emergency department database study
Snippet: The disruption of the blood-brain-barrier may be attributed to various conditions, one of which could be hypertension and a history of stroke, commonly observed in patients with SAE [37]. Hypertension and associated metabolic disturbances may constitute significant susceptibility factors for cognitive alterations and, consequently, risk factors for developing SAE. Understanding these associations can help clinicians identify high-risk patients, implement preventive measures, and tailor management strategies to optimize outcomes in SAE. 

We found that within the SAE group 15 patients (48.4%) had acute kidney injury (AKI), manifested by an increase in serum creatinine concentration and/or a decrease in urine output. However, statistically, we did not observe a significant difference between non-SAE and SAE patients. Nevertheless, the intense fluid resuscitation and diuretic treatment may attenuate the increase in serum creatinine level, making the diagnosis of this condition difficult and sometimes delayed. Globally, there is a growing incidence of sepsis-associated acute kidney injuries, currently ranging between 40 and 50% in the ICU [38]. It remains a major complication of sepsis among critically ill patients, associated with a poorer prognosis and increased morbidity [39]. 

Furthermore, we found that APACHE II score is associated with a higher mortality rate (p = 0.002) among E. coli urosepsis patients with SAE. The incidence of E. coli urosepsis complicated by SAE is associated with a poorer prognosis and worse outcomes. In our research the APACHE II score has been used as a predictor of increased mortality among SAE patients, highlighting the importance of general health condition and its correlation with the severity of sepsis. Both factors are closely related to the prevalence of encephalopathy. Our results are consistent with observations in recent research on sepsis-associated brain injury [6,22,40]. It is worth emphasizing that a GCS score <15 was required to classify a patient as having SAE, meanwhile the GCS score is also a component of the APACHE II score. This may introduce potential bias. 

The laboratory findings did not correlate significantly with the severity of urosepsis.

Snippet: Over recent decades, the incidence of sepsis in the United States has demonstrated a consistent upward trend, a phenomenon attributed to population aging, increased survival from chronic illnesses, greater use of invasive medical devices, and improved recognition and reporting of sepsis cases. Despite this rise in incidence, overall mortality from sepsis has declined, reflecting advances in early diagnosis, antimicrobial therapy, and critical care management. Nevertheless, urosepsis remains associated with substantial mortality, with reported death rates ranging from 30% to 40%, highlighting its clinical severity [5] [6]. Urosepsis accounts for a significant proportion of sepsis cases, particularly among hospitalized and elderly patients. The disease burden is further amplified by its frequent association with severe complications, including acute respiratory distress syndrome, acute kidney injury, and disseminated intravascular coagulopathy. These complications not only increase mortality risk but also contribute to prolonged hospital stays, higher healthcare costs, and long-term functional impairment among survivors [5][6]. Epidemiologic patterns suggest that the severity of urosepsis has increased over time, with patients presenting with more advanced organ dysfunction at the time of diagnosis. This trend may reflect delayed presentation, increasing antimicrobial resistance, or a higher prevalence of comorbid conditions. Urosepsis therefore represents an ongoing public health challenge, requiring sustained efforts in prevention, early detection, and comprehensive management strategies to reduce its impact on patient outcomes and healthcare systems.

Snippet: Organ failure is a hallmark of sepsis [1]. Kidney failure frequently occurs in sepsis, and sepsis is the most common etiology of acute kidney injury (AKI) [2]. AKI is not a single disease but a loose collection of syndromes as diverse as sepsis, cardiorenal syndrome, and urinary tract obstruction [3]. Sepsis encompass a spectrum of disorders involving both the heart and kidneys, in which acute or chronic dysfunction in one organ can induce acute or chronic dysfunction in another [4]. Even though the entire phenomenon of sepsis-associated AKI is not fully understood, its long-term adverse outcomes are related to multiple organ failures [5,6]. Because both sepsis and AKI are independently associated with adverse outcomes, the early detection of AKI is critical to provide opportunities for successful intervention and resuscitation in septic patients. 

The early detection of kidney failure by monitoring kidney function using injury and/or stress biomarkers would be crucial to decrease hospital mortality and the duration of hospital stays [7]. However, the current clinical diagnosis of kidney failure relies on markers such as glomerular filtration rate (GFR) based on increased serum creatinine (sCr) levels and decreased urine output [8,9]. In sepsis, the sequential (sepsis-related) organ failure assessment (SOFA) scoring system has been used to assess organ functions, and the sCr level is used to evaluate kidney function [10]. Changes in sCr levels or urine output are neither sensitive nor specific for AKI; the sCr level is also affected by numerous factors, and its solitary use might not reflect the actual degree of kidney function [3]. Moreover, the inverse relationship between GFR and sCr levels is nonlinear in patients with nearnormal kidney function [8]. Therefore, early and reliable biomarkers are required for critically ill septic patients at risk of developing AKI or likely to need clinical treatments, such as renal replacement therapy (RRT) [11].

Title: Risk Factors for Development of Acute Kidney Injury in Patients with Urinary Tract Infection
Snippet: Urinary tract infection (UTI) is one of the most common bacterial infections [1]. The overall annual incidence of UTI was 1.75% among residents of the Calgary Health Region, Canada during 2004-2005 [2]. The 2007 National Ambulatory Medical Care Surveys estimated UTIs were responsible for nearly two million visits to emergency departments annually in the USA [3]. 

UTI can be either asymptomatic or symptomatic, characterized by a wide spectrum of symptoms ranging from mild irritative voiding to bacteremia, sepsis, shock or even death. In specific patient groups, urosepsis may show high mortality rates of 25% to 60% [4]. 

Sepsis is one of the most common triggers of acute kidney injury (AKI) [5], and about 60% patients with septic shock developed AKI [6]. Acute UTI may cause sudden deterioration of renal function, especially for urinary tract obstruction [7]. AKI is associated with high morbidity and mortality during acute care [8][9][10]. Patients with severe AKI were under increased risk of end stage renal disease and even death after hospital discharge [11][12][13]. 

Since sepsis-related AKI leads to poor outcomes and increased healthcare costs, identification of the risk factors for development of AKI in patients with UTI is critical. However, there were few studies focusing on this important issue. In this retrospective study, we investigated the clinical characteristics and change of renal function to identify the risk factors for development of AKI in UTI patients.

Organ failure is a hallmark of sepsis [1]. Kidney failure frequently occurs in sepsis, and sepsis is the most common etiology of acute kidney injury (AKI) [2]. AKI is not a single disease but a loose collection of syndromes as diverse as sepsis, cardiorenal syndrome, and urinary tract obstruction [3]. Sepsis encompass a spectrum of disorders involving both the heart and kidneys, in which acute or chronic dysfunction in one organ can induce acute or chronic dysfunction in another [4]. Even though the entire phenomenon of sepsis-associated AKI is not fully understood, its long-term adverse outcomes are related to multiple organ failures [5,6]. Because both sepsis and AKI are independently associated with adverse outcomes, the early detection of AKI is critical to provide opportunities for successful intervention and resuscitation in septic patients. 

The early detection of kidney failure by monitoring kidney function using injury and/or stress biomarkers would be crucial to decrease hospital mortality and the duration of hospital stays [7]. However, the current clinical diagnosis of kidney failure relies on markers such as glomerular filtration rate (GFR) based on increased serum creatinine (sCr) levels and decreased urine output [8,9]. In sepsis, the sequential (sepsis-related) organ failure assessment (SOFA) scoring system has been used to assess organ functions, and the sCr level is used to evaluate kidney function [10]. Changes in sCr levels or urine output are neither sensitive nor specific for AKI; the sCr level is also affected by numerous factors, and its solitary use might not reflect the actual degree of kidney function [3]. Moreover, the inverse relationship between GFR and sCr levels is nonlinear in patients with nearnormal kidney function [8]. Therefore, early and reliable biomarkers are required for critically ill septic patients at risk of developing AKI or likely to need clinical treatments, such as renal replacement therapy (RRT) [11].

snippet.text:
Urinary tract infection (UTI) is one of the most common bacterial infections [1]. The overall annual incidence of UTI was 1.75% among residents of the Calgary Health Region, Canada during 2004-2005 [2]. The 2007 National Ambulatory Medical Care Surveys estimated UTIs were responsible for nearly two million visits to emergency departments annually in the USA [3]. 

UTI can be either asymptomatic or symptomatic, characterized by a wide spectrum of symptoms ranging from mild irritative voiding to bacteremia, sepsis, shock or even death. In specific patient groups, urosepsis may show high mortality rates of 25% to 60% [4]. 

Sepsis is one of the most common triggers of acute kidney injury (AKI) [5], and about 60% patients with septic shock developed AKI [6]. Acute UTI may cause sudden deterioration of renal function, especially for urinary tract obstruction [7]. AKI is associated with high morbidity and mortality during acute care [8][9][10]. Patients with severe AKI were under increased risk of end stage renal disease and even death after hospital discharge [11][12][13]. 

Since sepsis-related AKI leads to poor outcomes and increased healthcare costs, identification of the risk factors for development of AKI in patients with UTI is critical. However, there were few studies focusing on this important issue. In this retrospective study, we investigated the clinical characteristics and change of renal function to identify the risk factors for development of AKI in UTI patients.

documents.snippet: Over recent decades, the incidence of sepsis in the United States has demonstrated a consistent upward trend, a phenomenon attributed to population aging, increased survival from chronic illnesses, greater use of invasive medical devices, and improved recognition and reporting of sepsis cases. Despite this rise in incidence, overall mortality from sepsis has declined, reflecting advances in early diagnosis, antimicrobial therapy, and critical care management. Nevertheless, urosepsis remains associated with substantial mortality, with reported death rates ranging from 30% to 40%, highlighting its clinical severity [5] [6]. Urosepsis accounts for a significant proportion of sepsis cases, particularly among hospitalized and elderly patients. The disease burden is further amplified by its frequent association with severe complications, including acute respiratory distress syndrome, acute kidney injury, and disseminated intravascular coagulopathy. These complications not only increase mortality risk but also contribute to prolonged hospital stays, higher healthcare costs, and long-term functional impairment among survivors [5][6]. Epidemiologic patterns suggest that the severity of urosepsis has increased over time, with patients presenting with more advanced organ dysfunction at the time of diagnosis. This trend may reflect delayed presentation, increasing antimicrobial resistance, or a higher prevalence of comorbid conditions. Urosepsis therefore represents an ongoing public health challenge, requiring sustained efforts in prevention, early detection, and comprehensive management strategies to reduce its impact on patient outcomes and healthcare systems.
